overview.body: BUILD unit. Module 5 is one idea: classes. A class bundles data with the functions that work on it. In Module 4, each city lived in two dictionaries, and five library functions existed only to dig through them: display_destinations, get_destination, get_redirect, is_win_city, and is_dead_end. This lab you build a City class in a new file, city.py, turn the two dictionaries into one City object per city, and move those five functions into the class as methods. The game itself does not change: every run in this lab prints exactly what your Lab 4.3 printed. That is how you know the refactor worked.

mentorQuote.quote: Players will never see this lab, and that's the point. Same menus, same trivia, same beach. What changes is how the game is put together, so the next feature is easier to build. Next week the player gets the same treatment.

Define a City class in city.py: a constructor, four private attributes, accessors, and a mutator
Write build_cities(distances, city_info) to make one City object per city
Move display_destinations, get_destination, get_redirect, is_win_city, and is_dead_end into the class as methods, and call them on City objects
Give City a __str__ method and city.py a self-test
Prove the refactor: every run matches Lab 4.3, line for line
overview.keyConceptsText: A class is a blueprint; an object (an instance) is one thing built from it. City('Houston', 'GATEWAY', 'Space City') runs the class's __init__ method, which stores those values in the new object's attributes. An attribute whose name starts with two underscores, like self.__name, is private: code outside the class can't reach it, so it asks through methods. An accessor returns an attribute's value; a mutator changes it. Every method's first parameter is self, the object the method was called on: in houston.get_tagline(), self is houston. __str__ returns the text Python uses when you print an object or put it in an f-string. A refactor changes how code is organized without changing what it does.
overview.textbookReference: Chapter 10: Section 10.2 (Classes) covers class, __init__, self, hiding attributes, and __str__. Section 10.3 (Working with Instances) covers accessor and mutator methods and passing objects as arguments. Your BookEx programs: 10-9 and 10-10 (BankAccount), 10-12 and 10-13 (CellPhone).

content.body: A new file, city.py, holding a City class: a constructor that stores four private attributes, three accessors, and one mutator. Then build_cities() in lab-5-1.py turns your two dictionaries into one City object per city, and every stop asks its City for the tagline.

Right now one city's data is split across two dictionaries: its roads are in distances, and its type and tagline are in city_info. A City object holds all of it in one place. Its attributes are private, so code outside the class can't reach them directly; it asks through methods instead. That is encapsulation, and it is the main idea of Chapter 10.

One course rule on top of that: to show a number to a set number of decimal places, format it in an f-string, like f'{rate:.1f}', instead of using round(). Here's why: round() changes the number itself, while an f-string changes only what's shown, so the full value is still there for the math that comes later. Picture plotting a course from El Paso to San Antonio: about 500 miles on a steady heading of 108.77 degrees. Round the heading to 109 and you're off by less than a quarter of a degree, which sounds like nothing. Fly it anyway and you miss San Antonio by about 2 miles. Round on every leg of a longer trip and the misses can stack up. Keep the full number for the math, and display only what you print.
